# Tala patches to flutter_webrtc 1.6.3

Five changes: the camera start in `common/cpp/src/flutter_media_stream.cc` and its header, libwebrtc checksum verification in `third_party/CMakeLists.txt`, screen sharing through the portal, background blur with touch up, and noise cancellation (each in its own section below). `getUserMedia` opened the camera on the UI thread; on a Logitech QuickCam 3000 libwebrtc's 195 format probes took about 8s, which froze the window past GNOME's 5s "not responding" limit. The slow part now runs on a worker.

To upgrade: copy the new release here, reapply this change, or drop this directory if upstream fixes it. Worth offering upstream.

The prebuilt libwebrtc isn't committed. CMake downloads it at the version in `third_party/libwebrtc_version.ini` and checks the Linux x64 zip against `sha256_linux_x64` there, stopping the build on a mismatch. To upgrade libwebrtc, change the version and the checksum together. The build still fails if that release disappears from GitHub.

## Screen sharing through the portal (Linux)

libwebrtc's own desktop capture opens two portal sessions for one share (two pickers) and tells Dart neither when the user cancels nor when the share ends. Tala does the portal and PipeWire part itself instead:

- `linux/portal_screencast.{h,cc}`: one `org.freedesktop.portal.ScreenCast` session per share (CreateSession, SelectSources for screens and windows, Start, OpenPipeWireRemote), then a PipeWire stream of BGRx/RGBx shared-memory buffers converted to I420. The last picture is sent again each second while nothing changes, so someone who starts watching later gets one. Closing the object closes the session.
- `common/cpp/src/flutter_screen_capture.cc` and its header: `GetPortalDisplayMedia` makes a stream with a custom video source fed by the capture and returns it in `getDisplayMedia`'s shape; `StopPortalDisplayMedia` ends it. Outcomes go out on the event channel as `{"event": "portalScreenCast", "streamId", "state": "sharing|cancelled|stopped|failed"}`.
- `common/cpp/src/flutter_webrtc.cc`: the `getPortalDisplayMedia` and `stopPortalDisplayMedia` methods, Linux only.
- `lib/flutter_webrtc.dart`: exports `FlutterWebRTCEventChannel` and `MediaStreamNative` for the Dart side (`lib/src/screen_share.dart` in Tala).
- `linux/CMakeLists.txt`: builds it, linking `libpipewire-0.3` and `gio-unix-2.0` through pkg-config. Building needs `libpipewire-0.3-dev`.

Worth offering upstream: it fixes the two-picker problem for every Linux user of the plugin.

## Background blur, pictures and touch up (Linux)

The libwebrtc build already lets an `RTCVideoProcessor` change every local frame before it's encoded or shown, and `FlutterWebRTCBase::AddVideoProcessor` attaches one to a track. Tala adds the processor and a method to switch it:

- `linux/selfie_segmenter.{h,cc}`: runs MediaPipe's landscape selfie segmenter (Apache License 2.0, Google) with a small engine of Tala's own, no inference library. `linux/selfie_model_data.inc` holds the model's layers and float16 weights, generated by `tool/blur/export_selfie_model.py` from the pinned `.tflite`.
- `linux/background_blur.{h,cc}`: I420 in, I420 out. Shrinks the frame for the model and smooths the mask over frames, then refines it against the picture with a guided filter at about 640 wide (the model's 256-wide mask is too coarse for a 720p edge), blurs only the background of a small copy, weighted by the mask so the person leaves no halo, and blends. No WebRTC or GTK, so `tool/blur/check_segmenter.py` (against Google's runtime) and `tool/blur/check_blur.py` (timing and a picture) build and run it with plain g++.
  With a picture set (`SetPicture`, RGBA), the background is replaced instead: the picture is cropped to the frame's shape and scaled once per frame size, and the mask's lowest 30% is counted as background, since that fringe carries the real room's color.
  Touch up (`SetLook`, 0 to 1) smooths the person's skin before any of that: each pixel where the refined mask says person and the chroma says skin (the usual Cb 77 to 127, Cr 133 to 173 box, eased) is pulled toward a self-guided filter of the brightness at the guide's size, by at most 70%, and only as far as it differs from it by a little, so pores and shine go while eyes, brows and the edges of hair and glasses stay. With `blur` false and no picture, the background is left as it was.
- `linux/gpu_effects.{h,cc}`: everything after the person model on the GPU, through OpenGL ES 3 on a window-less EGL context (EGL's device platform, then Mesa's surfaceless one), reached through libepoxy: no vendor API and nothing to link but libepoxy, which GTK needs anyway. `Create` refuses software renderers (llvmpipe and the like), contexts without OpenGL ES 3 or `GL_EXT_color_buffer_float`, and shaders that don't build. The shaders sample with `texelFetch` and repeat `background_blur.cc`'s arithmetic (its `Axis` bilinear, rounding, order of steps), so the two engines agree to within one level on a few pixels; outputs are packed four pixels to an RGBA8 texel and read back as the planes' bytes. `linux/effects_tuning.h` holds the numbers both use.
  `BackgroundBlur` tries the GPU on its first frame. Each kind of look (picture, blur, touch up) is first done both ways on one frame, the CPU's picture going out; more than 0.1% of bytes apart by over 2 drops the GPU for good, as does any GL error (that frame is redone on the CPU) or the GPU averaging slower than the CPU's check frame over 30 frames. `Engine()` says which is in use and why.
- `linux/blur_processor.h`: the `RTCVideoProcessor` around it. A new picture is handed over under a mutex and taken up on the next frame.
- `common/cpp/src/flutter_webrtc.cc` and its header: `getBackgroundEngine` (`trackId`; the engine string, or null) and the `setBackgroundBlur` method (`trackId`, `enabled`, optional `picture` bytes with `width` and `height`, optional `blur` (default true; false leaves the background alone when there's no picture) and `touchUp` (0 to 1); returns whether the processor is attached; calling again on an attached track switches), Linux only. Processors are freed when turned off, when their track is gone, and in the destructor.
- `linux/CMakeLists.txt`: builds the new sources, links libepoxy and threads.

Tala asks for 1080p at up to 60 fps, so the full-size passes (blending, touch up), the guided filter's box blurs and the three planes' blurs are split across up to four threads (`ParallelRows`), and the model runs at most every 25 ms (every other frame at 60 fps; the mask is smoothed over frames anyway). The output is byte for byte what one thread gives. On a Ryzen 7 3700X at 1920x1080 and 60 fps, a frame takes about 13 ms with blur, 11 ms with a picture, 13 ms with touch up alone and 17 ms with touch up and blur (just under 60 fps), costing about 1.7, 1.3, 1.2 and 2.3 cores; at 30 fps about 0.95, 0.8, 0.7 and 1.25 cores. Threads cost about a quarter more processor time than one thread doing the same work. `tool/blur/check_blur_main.cc --fps=60 --cpu` times it that way. On the GPU (an RTX 2080 on NVIDIA's 595 driver) every look takes about 5 ms a frame and about 0.37 cores at 60 fps, most of it the model; `--compare` checks GPU against CPU (tried at 640x480, 1279x719, 1280x720, 1366x768, 1920x1080 and 3840x2160: at most one level apart). Forced onto Mesa there, it found only llvmpipe and stayed on the CPU, and a deliberately broken shader was caught by the check.

## Noise cancellation (Linux)

The libwebrtc build gives `RTCAudioProcessing::SetCapturePostProcessing`, which hands a custom processor each 10 ms of microphone audio after WebRTC's own echo, noise and gain handling and before encoding: the first channel, at the processing rate (48 kHz from a desktop mic), as floats scaled to 16 bits. Tala's processor runs Xiph's RNNoise on it.

- `third_party/rnnoise/`: RNNoise 0.2 (BSD 3-clause), from the release tarball `rnnoise-0.2.tar.gz` (sha256 `90fce4b00b9ff24c08dbfe31b82ffd43bae383d85c5535676d28b0a2b11c0d37`): `COPYING`, `AUTHORS`, `include/rnnoise.h`, and from `src/` the ten library sources with all headers, including `rnnoise_data.c`, the default model's weights. Unchanged. Built as its own static library (`tala_rnnoise`) with plain C and SSE2, symbols hidden.
- `linux/noise_suppressor.{h,cc}`: 10 ms in place. 48 kHz goes straight to RNNoise; 16 and 32 kHz are stretched to 48 kHz by straight lines and sampled back. No WebRTC, so `tool/noise/check_noise.py` builds and checks it with g++ against speech and noise.
- `linux/noise_processor.h`: the `CustomProcessing`, switched with `SetEnabled`. libwebrtc's adapter calls `Initialize` on whatever processor it holds, so setting nullptr after the first call would crash it; the processor is therefore set once and never freed.
- `common/cpp/src/flutter_webrtc.cc` and its header: `setNoiseCancellation` (`enabled`; returns whether it's on) and `getNoiseCancellation` (`enabled`, and `working` once the audio thread has cleaned audio since it was turned on). It applies to every microphone track, since there's one audio processing module.
- `linux/CMakeLists.txt`: enables C, builds `tala_rnnoise` and `noise_suppressor.cc`.

On a Ryzen 7 3700X it takes about 0.14 ms per 10 ms (1.4% of one core) and delays the audio by 20 ms. On ALSA's spoken test sounds with a fan and keyboard clicks about 13 dB below, speech comes through within 0.2 dB and the noise between words drops by about 28 dB.
